text: dbatools gives you commands, but a real environment usually has dozens of instances, not one. Once you need to run the same script against many servers, or run something that has to execute on the server itself, you need PowerShell Remoting, not just a dbatools connection.

PowerShell Remoting runs on WinRM, Windows Remote Management, listening on port 5985 or 5986. Enable-PSRemoting starts the service, creates a listener, and opens the firewall rule. It's not magic, it's an HTTP-based management protocol underneath Invoke-Command.

Invoke-Command runs a script block on one or more remote computers and returns the results to you. Because the block executes on each remote machine, this is the tool for tasks about the server itself, not for a plain dbatools call, which just talks to SQL Server over the network.

The pattern DBAs reach for most: run one dbatools command against every server in an estate, from a single script, with no RDP session opened anywhere. Notice SqlInstance localhost inside the block — it's local from that remote machine's own point of view.

Remoting gets your code running on the right box; dbatools does the actual SQL Server work once it's there. Next up: SMO, the .NET API dbatools itself is partly built on, for the jobs that don't have a dedicated dbatools command.
